title: Week 17 · Lesson 41: Psychiatric Pharmacology I — Depression, Anxiety, Sleep & Medication Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 17 — Lesson 41: Psychiatric Pharmacology I — Depression, Anxiety, Sleep & Medication Safety

FNP-level goal: Select and monitor common psychiatric medications through a diagnosis-first, safety-first framework that includes suicide risk, bipolar-spectrum screening, substance use, sleep, medical mimics, and clear referral thresholds.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate unipolar depression, bipolar-spectrum illness, anxiety disorders, insomnia, substance effects, and medical mimics before medication selection.
  • Compare common antidepressant classes by expected benefits, adverse effects, interactions, and patient-specific fit.
  • Screen for mania/hypomania and suicide risk before and after an antidepressant change.
  • Recognize sedative burden, benzodiazepine risk, and sleep-medication safety issues.
  • Create a measurement-based follow-up and escalation plan.
  • Identify psychiatric emergencies that need immediate evaluation.

Part 1 — A Medication Does Not Establish the Diagnosis

Depressed mood, anxiety, poor concentration, irritability, insomnia, fatigue, and appetite change can reflect major depression, bipolar disorder, PTSD, panic disorder, substance use, grief, thyroid disease, anemia, sleep apnea, medication effects, chronic pain, delirium, or psychosis. Do not choose an antidepressant simply because a patient requests “something for anxiety.”

Begin with duration, severity, impairment, prior episodes, family history, current/past mania or hypomania, psychosis, trauma, substance use, pregnancy potential, medical conditions, medication list, and immediate safety assessment.

Part 2 — Safety Comes Before Symptom Scores

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, intent, plan, access to lethal means, prior attempts, self-harm, violence risk, psychosis, severe agitation, inability to care for self, intoxication/withdrawal, and protective factors. A screening tool supports care but does not replace a clinical risk assessment.

Imminent suicide risk, inability to maintain safety, command hallucinations, severe mania, psychosis with unsafe behavior, or marked functional collapse requires emergency evaluation. Do not rely on a routine follow-up appointment or portal message in an unstable situation.

Part 3 — Screen for Bipolar Spectrum Before Antidepressant Monotherapy

A history of decreased need for sleep with increased energy, elevated or markedly irritable mood, pressured speech, racing thoughts, impulsive spending/sexual risk, grandiosity, or episodic unusually high goal-directed activity may suggest mania or hypomania. Family history and prior antidepressant-associated activation also matter.

Antidepressant monotherapy can be unsafe or ineffective when bipolar disorder is the true illness. Suspected bipolar disorder, psychosis, complex comorbidity, or diagnostic uncertainty merits psychiatric consultation and a tailored plan.

Part 4 — Antidepressants: Choose for the Patient, Not the Brand

SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine, and other options have different adverse-effect and interaction profiles. Selection considers prior response, target symptoms, sleep, appetite, sexual adverse effects, anxiety activation, blood pressure, seizure risk, cardiac/QT context, liver/kidney function, other serotonergic drugs, cost, pregnancy/lactation context, and patient preference.

Explain that antidepressant response is not immediate. Early adverse effects can occur before meaningful benefit. Set a follow-up plan that assesses adherence, side effects, safety, symptom change, and function rather than giving an indefinite refill.

Part 5 — SSRIs and SNRIs: Common Does Not Mean Simple

SSRIs and SNRIs are commonly used for depressive and anxiety disorders. Potential concerns include GI effects, sexual dysfunction, sleep change, activation, discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly, bleeding-risk context with NSAIDs/anticoagulants, and serotonin toxicity with interacting agents. SNRIs may also require blood-pressure and other patient-specific monitoring.

Medication changes should be deliberate. Ask about OTC products, supplements, migraine drugs, stimulants, analgesics, and other prescribers before combining serotonergic medications.

Part 6 — Serotonin Toxicity: Recognize the Pattern

Serotonin toxicity is a clinical syndrome that can occur with serotonergic medication combinations, dose changes, or interactions. Concerning findings can include agitation, confusion, tremor, hyperreflexia/clonus, diaphoresis, diarrhea, fever, and autonomic instability. Severity varies, but a systemically ill or unstable patient needs urgent evaluation.

Do not advise a patient with concerning neuromuscular and autonomic symptoms to simply “wait for the medication to adjust.”

Part 7 — Bupropion and Mirtazapine: Match Benefits and Risks

Bupropion can be a useful option in selected contexts but requires assessment of seizure risk, eating-disorder history, activation, and other contraindications. Mirtazapine may be considered when sleep or appetite effects are clinically relevant, while also requiring discussion of sedation and weight/metabolic considerations.

These are examples of symptom-targeted selection—not a shortcut around diagnosis, psychotherapy, social stressors, or safety assessment.

Part 8 — Anxiety: Medication Is One Component of Care

Anxiety treatment may include psychotherapy, behavioral skills, sleep support, treatment of substance use, and medication when indicated. Confirm whether symptoms are generalized anxiety, panic, trauma-related, medication-induced, hyperthyroid-related, cardiopulmonary, or due to another condition.

For panic-like symptoms, evaluate chest pain, syncope, arrhythmia, stimulant exposure, pulmonary disease, and thyroid symptoms as appropriate. Do not diagnose panic solely because initial testing is unrevealing.

Part 9 — Benzodiazepines: Short-Term Relief, Long-Term Risk

Benzodiazepines can cause sedation, falls, cognitive impairment, dependence, withdrawal, and dangerous additive respiratory/CNS depression with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives. They are not a casual long-term answer to insomnia or chronic anxiety.

For a patient already taking a benzodiazepine long term, do not abruptly discontinue it except in an emergency requiring immediate action. Reassess benefit and risk, coordinate care, and use an individualized, guideline-informed tapering approach when risks outweigh benefits.

Part 10 — Insomnia: Treat the Driver, Not Just the Night

Insomnia may arise from depression, anxiety, trauma, pain, medication effects, caffeine/stimulants, alcohol, sleep apnea, restless legs, circadian disruption, or acute stress. Sedatives can worsen falls, cognition, respiratory risk, and next-day performance.

Assess sleep schedule, snoring/apnea symptoms, daytime sleepiness, mood, substances, and safety-sensitive work. Behavioral treatment and sleep-focused interventions are foundational; medication, if used, needs a defined indication, duration, and monitoring plan.

Part 11 — Antidepressant Follow-Up Is Active Monitoring

At initiation and after medication changes, arrange follow-up appropriate to severity and risk. Review suicidal thinking, activation, mania symptoms, adherence, emerging adverse effects, substance use, functional change, and barriers to therapy. Young adults, adolescents, and people with new/worsening agitation require particularly attentive monitoring consistent with medication warnings and clinical context.

“No side effects” is not the only success marker. Ask whether the patient is safer, sleeping, functioning, attending work/school, and able to use therapy or coping strategies.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Depression or Bipolar Disorder?

A 31-year-old requests an antidepressant for depression. On further history, they report prior periods of sleeping three hours nightly for a week while feeling unusually energized, starting several projects, spending excessively, and later “crashing.”

FNP reasoning: episodic decreased need for sleep + increased energy/goal-directed behavior + risky spending raises bipolar-spectrum concern. Do not reflexively begin antidepressant monotherapy; assess safety and obtain psychiatric support.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Anxiety With Medical Red Flags

A 58-year-old attributes sudden palpitations, chest pressure, diaphoresis, and near-syncope to panic. They have diabetes and hypertension.

Do not anchor on anxiety. Cardiopulmonary and ischemic causes require immediate consideration and appropriate emergency evaluation. A psychiatric medication cannot make this presentation safe.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: Sedative Stacking

An older adult taking an opioid for chronic pain requests a benzodiazepine for sleep. They have COPD and two recent falls.

Build the risk: opioid + benzodiazepine + COPD + falls → increased sedation and respiratory-depression risk. Assess immediate safety, avoid casual sedative stacking, address the sleep driver, and develop safer alternatives and follow-up.

FNP Psychiatric Medication Framework

  1. Confirm the syndrome and screen for medical/substance causes.
  2. Assess suicide, violence, psychosis, mania, withdrawal, and ability to maintain safety.
  3. Choose medication based on diagnosis, target symptoms, comorbidities, interactions, and patient priorities.
  4. Explain expected timeline, early adverse effects, serious warning symptoms, and medication adherence/discontinuation risks.
  5. Use measurement-based follow-up with functional and safety outcomes.
  6. Escalate urgently for imminent safety risk, psychosis, severe mania, delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, or possible medical emergency.

High-Yield Summary

Before antidepressants: screen for bipolar-spectrum symptoms and suicide risk.
SSRIs/SNRIs: require interaction, activation, discontinuation, bleeding-risk, and patient-specific monitoring.
Benzodiazepines: can cause dependence, falls, and dangerous additive sedation; do not stop chronic use abruptly without a safe plan.
Insomnia: needs evaluation of its driver; sedatives are not a default long-term solution.
Psychiatric emergencies: suicide risk, psychosis, severe mania, inability to care for self, and intoxication/withdrawal need urgent action.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Psychiatric diagnosis, psychotropic medication selection, dosing, tapering, controlled-substance management, suicide-risk assessment, and referral must follow current guidelines, prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
